title: Training Process: Overview
text:
Training Process: Overview
• Goal: optimize parameters θ = {W , b} to minimize loss L.
• Direct minimization is infeasible due to:
• Non-linear models (e.g., deep networks).
• High-dimensional parameter space.
• Solution: iterative procedure based on gradients.

Training Process: Overview
• Goal: optimize parameters θ = {W , b} to minimize loss L.
• Direct minimization is infeasible due to:
• Non-linear models (e.g., deep networks).
• High-dimensional parameter space.
• Solution: iterative procedure based on gradients.

title: Why Three Steps?
text:
Why Three Steps?
• Forward pass: compute predictions ˆy and evaluate loss L.
• Backward pass: compute gradients ∇θL via backpropagation.
• Update step: adjust parameters θ using an optimizer (e.g., SGD,
Adam).
Key Idea
Splitting into 3 steps ensures:
• Clear separation of computation and optimization.
• Efficient reuse of intermediate activations.
• Scalable training for large models.

title: Chain Rule and Backpropagation
text:
Chain Rule and Backpropagation
Key Idea
Gradients flow backward through the computational graph. For each
parameter w on the path from input to loss:
∂L
∂w = ∂L
∂ˆy · ∂ˆy
∂z1
· ∂z1
∂z2
· · · · ∂zk
∂w
Each term is a local derivative; the chain rule multiplies them along the path.
• Frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) compute this automatically via
autograd.
• Understanding the idea helps debug gradients and design custom layers.

mini-batch size B.
1 Initialize parameters θ.
2 for epoch = 1 to E do

title: Notes on Training Terminology
text:
Notes on Training Terminology
Key Concepts
• Mini-batch: a small subset of the training dataset used in one
forward–backward–update cycle. Balances efficiency and gradient
stability.
• Epoch: one complete pass through the entire training dataset (all
mini-batches).
• Iteration (step): one update of parameters using a single mini-batch.
• Learning rate η: step size for parameter updates; too large ⇒
divergence, too small ⇒slow convergence.
• Momentum: technique to smooth updates by accumulating past
gradients, reducing oscillations.
• Learning rate schedule: strategy to adjust η during training (e.g.,
decay, cosine annealing).

title: SGD with Momentum — Update
text:
SGD with Momentum — Update
Formula
gt = ∇θLt(θ),
vt = µvt−1 + gt,
θ ←θ −η vt
• θ: parameter vector (e.g., {W , b}).
• gt: gradient on current mini-batch.
• vt: momentum (velocity) vector.
• Initialization: set v0 = 0 at the beginning of training.
Note
vt is recursive: each update depends on previous momentum vt−1. Initialization with
zero is standard; after several steps, vt accumulates a smoothed history of past
gradients.

title: SGD with Momentum — Intuition
text:
SGD with Momentum — Intuition
Why Momentum?
• Accumulates a running direction (inertia).
• Dampens oscillations across steep directions.
• Accelerates along shallow valleys.
• More stable than vanilla SGD in ill-conditioned landscapes.

title: AdaGrad — Intuition
text:
AdaGrad — Intuition
Why AdaGrad?
• Adapts learning rate for each parameter individually.
• Frequent features ⇒smaller effective step size. Infrequent features ⇒larger
effective step size.
• Naturally well-suited for sparse data (e.g., text / NLP).

title: AdaGrad — Usage
text:
AdaGrad — Usage
Practical Notes
• Good choice for sparse features or embeddings.
• Main drawback: effective learning rate decays monotonically, can stall long
training.
• Rarely used for deep networks today; mostly replaced by RMSProp/Adam.
• Still relevant in NLP and recommendation tasks with sparse gradients.

title: RMSProp — Intuition
text:
RMSProp — Intuition
Why RMSProp?
• Fixes AdaGrad’s issue of monotonically decaying learning rates.
• Maintains a moving average of squared gradients.
• Effectively adapts learning rate per parameter in non-stationary problems.
• Provides more stable training for deep neural nets.

• Popular choice before Adam; still used in reinforcement learning.
• Tune η and ρ carefully; defaults often η = 0.001, ρ = 0.9.
• Consider combining with momentum for improved stability.

• Can overfit or lead to poor generalization without weight decay.
• Often combined with learning rate schedules (cosine decay, warmup).
• For vision models (CNNs, transformers), AdamW (decoupled weight decay) is
preferred.

title: AdamW — Intuition
text:
AdamW — Intuition
Why AdamW?
• In Adam, adding L2 regularization inside the loss couples it with adaptive step
sizes →suboptimal.
• AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient update.
• This yields better control of regularization and significantly improves
generalization.

title: SAM: Sharpness-Aware Minimization
text:
SAM: Sharpness-Aware Minimization
Objective: prefer flat minima by penalizing sharpness.
Mechanism: inner ascent to worst-case in a neighborhood, then descent.
Pros: better generalization; Cost: ≈2× compute per step.
Variants: ASAM, GSAM; can wrap around SGD/AdamW.

title: Summary & Choosing the Optimizer
text:
Summary & Choosing the Optimizer
• General default: AdamW + cosine LR + warmup; tune weight decay.
• Vision (from-scratch CNNs): SGD + Momentum often best
generalization.
• Large-batch pretraining: LAMB (or AdamW + careful scaling) +
warmup.
• Sparse features / NLP classic: AdaGrad / RMSProp still relevant.
• Flat minima / robustness: SAM (wrap your base optimizer).
• Memory-limited large models: Adafactor; New trials: Lion.
Practical Tips
Schedule matters (cosine, step, one-cycle); always try warmup.
Tune η first, then decay/momentum; log training curves and validate
frequently.

title: Regularization: Dropout
text:
Regularization: Dropout
Mechanism
During training: randomly set each neuron output to zero with probability p (e.g.,
0.1–0.5). At test time: use all neurons (scale by 1 −p if needed).
• Prevents co-adaptation: forces network to not rely on any single neuron
• Interpreted as training an ensemble of sub-networks
• Often applied after hidden layers; less common in modern transformers
(LayerNorm + augmentation preferred)

title: Normalization
text:
Normalization
Why?
Stabilize training by reducing internal covariate shift.
• BatchNorm: normalize activations across batch. Works well for CNNs;
depends on batch size.
• LayerNorm: normalize across features per sample. Common in transformers;
independent of batch size.
Notes
Normalization smooths the optimization landscape, allows larger η, and improves
convergence.

title: Early Stopping
text:
Early Stopping
Idea
Stop training when validation error no longer decreases (to avoid overfitting).
• Monitor validation loss or accuracy each epoch.
• If no improvement for p epochs (patience), stop training.
• Save best model weights (checkpointing).
Notes
Simple and effective; acts as a form of implicit regularization.

title: Practical Considerations — Initialization
text:
Practical Considerations — Initialization
Initialization
• Proper weight initialization stabilizes variance across layers.
• Xavier (Glorot): suitable for sigmoid/tanh activations.
• He (Kaiming): designed for ReLU and variants.

title: Practical Considerations — Gradients
text:
Practical Considerations — Gradients
Vanishing Gradients
• Gradients shrink as they backprop through deep networks.
• Mitigation: ReLU activations, residual connections, normalization layers.
Exploding Gradients
• Gradients grow uncontrollably, causing unstable updates.
• Mitigation: gradient clipping, careful initialization.

title: Practical Considerations — Batch Size
text:
Practical Considerations — Batch Size
Batch Size Trade-off
• Small batches: noisier updates, slower throughput, often better generalization.
• Large batches: faster throughput, smoother gradients, but risk poorer
generalization. Requires careful learning rate scaling (linear scaling rule).

title: Training Neural Networks: Summary
text:
Training Neural Networks: Summary
Key Points
• Training loop consists of:
• Forward pass: compute predictions.
• Loss computation: measure error vs. ground truth.
• Backward pass: compute gradients (backpropagation).
• Update step: adjust weights with optimizer.
• Choice of optimizer, learning rate schedule, and regularization strongly
influences convergence and generalization.
• Validation monitoring is essential to detect overfitting and apply early stopping.
Pipeline:
Data →Forward →Loss →Backward →Update →Repeat
